tools.name: CoMaps
tools.blurb: CoMaps is a community-run fork of Organic Maps and Maps.me that searches, routes, and speaks turn-by-turn directions with no mobile data, keeps hiking trails and offline Wikipedia articles on the phone, states plainly that it does not identify you, track you, or collect information, and is free for everyone through Google Play, F-Droid, the iOS App Store, the Mac App Store, and Flathub; the caveat is coverage, since its public transit layer reaches only a growing list of cities, so check your own before you rely on it.

tools.name: Lightworks
tools.blurb: Lightworks is a long-running video editor whose free tier, listed at zero on the company's own pricing page, includes timeline editing, automatic saving, advanced transitions, and simple visual effects on Windows, macOS, and Linux, and XDA's Nolen Jonker says it replaced his Premiere Pro subscription outright, with no watermark, an installer under 100MB, proxy files for modest hardware, and background rendering while you work; the catch is stated on that same pricing page, since free exports stop at 720p and some Linux functionality is restricted.

tools.name: Simplenote
tools.kind: iOS app, also Mac, Windows, web
tools.blurb: Simplenote is Automattic's free note app, and its App Store listing shows version 4.55 holding a 4.7 average from more than 4,300 ratings while it handles notes, to-do lists, and memos in markdown with tags, pins, instant search, version history, passcode or biometric lock, widgets, and shared notes; XDA's Yash Patel counts Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and a web app in the same free tier and is straight that Simplenote carries no databases, backlinks, plugins, or knowledge-management scaffolding, and the listing itself puts the last iPhone update on November 4, 2024, so take it as a stable plain place to write rather than a system that will keep growing new features.

tools.name: Obsidian
tools.blurb: Obsidian sits at the opposite end of the shelf from Simplenote: the app itself is free with no sign-up, and XDA's Patrick Hearn stacks the MediaDB, StoryLine, Visual Notes, and Web Clipper plugins on top of it to keep an offline books-and-films log, draft a novel where Scrivener used to sit, storyboard projects on a canvas, and search fifteen years of published articles by keyword; the honest accounting is that the official pricing page charges $4 a month billed annually (or $5 monthly) for Sync across devices and $8 a month per site for Publish, an optional commercial license runs $50 a year per user, and Hearn concedes these setups do not really solve a hard problem so much as gather everything into one window.

tools.name: EasySwitch
tools.blurb: EasySwitch joins the computers on one desk so a single keyboard and mouse slide between them, the clipboard carries text, images, and files up to 10MB across, and a second machine can act as an extra display, working in any combination of macOS 13 or later, Windows 10 and 11, and Linux, with end-to-end encryption included on the free tier rather than sold as an upgrade; the limits are stated plainly on the product page, since it runs over your local network only, the free tier stops at two computers while Pro is $49 once for up to five, Linux on X11 can receive a virtual display but cannot create one, and Windows 11 wants a driver installed the first time you use the display feature.

tools.name: Todoist
tools.blurb: XDA's Chandraveer Mathur left Google Keep for Todoist because its open API and integrations let him build automations around his tasks instead of retyping them, working from projects, nested subtasks, P1 to P4 priorities, natural-language dates, and saved filters; the honest catch is the move itself, since he reports Todoist does not readily accept imports and he copied across what he needed by hand, and Todoist's own pricing page caps the free Beginner plan at 5 personal projects, 3 filter views, and one week of activity history.

tools.name: HeliBoard
tools.blurb: HeliBoard is a keyboard built on the AOSP and OpenBoard code that ships with no internet permission at all, sitting at version 4.0 on F-Droid since July 12, 2026 with about 5,900 GitHub stars, and it brings local dictionaries, themes, clipboard history, and multilingual typing; Android Police's Oluwaniyi Raji is direct that its autocorrect is less accurate than Gboard's because it does not do contextual correction, which is why he found himself reading his own sentences again, and the project itself notes that glide typing works only if you supply a closed-source library it cannot ship.

tools.name: SD Maid 2/SE
tools.blurb: SD Maid 2/SE is a GPL 3.0 Android maintenance app with roughly 7,400 GitHub stars, distributed through the Play Store, F-Droid, IzzyOnDroid, and GitHub releases, whose CorpseFinder, AppCleaner, Deduplicator, Swiper, and Media Squeeze tools go after the residual folders, caches, expansion files, and logs an ordinary file manager never shows you; Android Police's Akshay Bhalla recovered about 6GB with the paid AppCleaner, which he prices at $3 a year or $6 for a lifetime license, and he warns you to audit the list before you confirm, because a file the scanner calls junk can be a document you still want.

tools.name: uBlock Origin Lite
tools.blurb: The Manifest V3 rewrite of the best known content blocker now has 17,000,000 users and a 4.5 rating from 3,400 reviews, and it blocks ads, trackers, and miners declaratively using uBlock Origin's own filters plus EasyList, EasyPrivacy, and Peter Lowe's server list, with more rulesets available in its options; Android Authority's Andrew Grush is blunt that the lite build gives up custom filters, dynamic filtering, the element picker, and malware protection, so it suits a casual user rather than someone who tuned the original by hand.

tools.name: RustDesk
tools.blurb: RustDesk is an open-source remote desktop app with about 121,700 GitHub stars that connects out of the box through the project's relay servers, or through a server you run yourself, so you can fix a relative's computer or reach your own without a subscription; MakeUseOf's Tashreef Shareef points out that it carries no commercial-use nag screens, no session time limits, and a built-in file transfer mode, then adds the fair warning that it is not built for latency-sensitive work like gaming or video, and that the advanced server features sit behind the paid Server Pro tier.

tools.name: Breezy Weather
tools.blurb: Breezy Weather pulls forecasts, observations, nowcasting, air quality, pollen, and alerts from more than 50 weather sources into a home screen you arrange yourself, with 13 widget options, no advertisements, and no news feed, and it has gathered 11,100 stars on GitHub; the catch is distribution, because the developer keeps it off the Play Store on purpose, so you install it from GitHub, F-Droid, IzzyOnDroid, or Obtainium, updates are manual unless you let Obtainium check every six hours, and Android Authority notes some phones need a setting like Samsung's Auto Blocker turned off first.

tools.name: Tab Notes
tools.blurb: Tab Notes replaces the new tab page with a plain writing surface that handles rich text and markdown, keeps a small drawing canvas for a diagram, and exports to .txt or .md, storing everything on the machine unless you connect your own Google Drive, with no third-party servers, tracking, or ads; it is also young and small, version 2.0.2 shipped on August 16 with 491 users and a 3.8 rating from 18 reviews, so treat it as a scratchpad rather than the only copy of anything you cannot lose.

tools.name: UniGetUI
tools.blurb: UniGetUI is one window over WinGet, Scoop, Chocolatey, and the other package managers already on a Windows PC, so a single screen shows everything with an update waiting and installs or removes it without hunting for download pages; the project is candid that the packages come from third-party publishers, so install only from names you trust, and that some WinGet packages still fail and have to be chased down in PowerShell.

tools.name: SubtitleGenerator
tools.blurb: Drop in a video and it transcribes, flags the words it is unsure about, lets you fix text and timing, styles the captions, and exports, all in one browser tab, with your video file staying on your device and only the audio sent off for transcription; the free tier is capped at 60 minutes of subtitle time a month and 10 minutes per video, and free exports top out at 720p with a small watermark.

tools.name: debloat.dev
tools.blurb: A community directory of open-source replacements for the software that ships with hardware, sorted into ten categories including printers and scanners, peripherals, smart home, NAS and storage, and phone sync, and it keeps no tracking and no cookies unless you sign in; the listings are submitted and rated by users rather than tested by an editor, so check a project's own repository for recent activity before you install it.

tools.name: Image Toolbox
tools.blurb: Image Toolbox is one Android app for the jobs most people keep eight apps for, resizing and converting pictures, stripping EXIF data, removing backgrounds, editing PDFs, stitching images, making GIFs, generating QR codes, and building collages, free under Apache 2.0 from the Play Store, F-Droid, or GitHub with no advertisements; the honest limits are that it is Android only, wants Android 7.0 or newer, and Android Authority's Yash Wate found it needs a pass through its settings, including Launcher Mode and the output folder, before it feels productive.

tools.name: FUTO Voice Input
tools.blurb: FUTO Voice Input takes over the microphone key on an Android keyboard and does the speech recognition on the phone itself with nothing stored, free from the Play Store, F-Droid, or a roughly 70 MB download, with an optional one-time license that also covers FUTO Keyboard; How-To Geek's Bertel King is candid about the tradeoff, because you cannot speak punctuation or delete by voice, it can stop listening during a pause unless you turn on auto-stop on silence, and it garbled a product name, hearing Wispr Flow as whisper flow.

tools.name: Plane
tools.blurb: Plane is an open-source tracker for projects, work items, cycles, and roadmaps, licensed AGPL v3 with about 57,200 stars on GitHub, and its free plan costs nothing per seat for as many as 12 people, each with 500 AI credits; the caveats are the ceiling and the setup, since a thirteenth teammate moves you to the $6 per seat Pro plan, and hosting it yourself means Docker or Kubernetes rather than an installer you double-click.

tools.name: Scribus
tools.blurb: Scribus is a page layout program for the jobs Microsoft Publisher used to do, brochures, books, and business cards, with color separations, CMYK and spot colors, ICC color management, and commercial grade PDF and PostScript output, free under the GNU GPL on Windows, macOS, Linux, BSD, and ChromeOS; the caveat is the move itself, because XDA's Patrick Hearn found an interface that looks like a product of 2001 and no Microsoft Office integration, and Microsoft's own support page says 365 subscribers lose access to Publisher after October 1, 2026 and tells you to convert your files to another format first, so expect a learning curve rather than a clean import.

tools.name: Kagi Search paywall filter
tools.blurb: Kagi's changelog entry dated August 21, 2026 says the search engine added a setting for removing paywalled links from search results automatically, which spares you the click into an article you cannot finish reading; the caveat is the price, because Kagi is a subscription search engine, its free trial stops at 100 searches and 100 Assistant interactions, and the paid tiers run from Starter at $5 a month for 300 searches to Professional at $10 a month for unlimited searches and Ultimate at $25 a month.

tools.name: HyNote for Mac
tools.blurb: HyNote records system and meeting audio on the Mac itself, so no meeting bot joins your Zoom, Teams, Meet, or Webex call, and it hands back a live transcript plus a summary with key points and action items, though its own setup steps have you sign in before recording and the free plan stops a session at 120 minutes, with paid tiers starting at $6.66 a month.

tools.name: career-ops
tools.blurb: career-ops turns an AI coding CLI into a job search desk that scores a listing against your CV on a one to five rubric, tailors an ATS-ready PDF, researches the company, and tracks every application in one place, but it needs Node.js plus a separate AI CLI to run, it never submits an application for you, and its own README warns that models may hallucinate skills you do not have.

tools.name: OpenLogi
tools.blurb: OpenLogi remaps Logitech buttons, DPI, SmartShift, gestures, and lighting from your own machine with no cloud account and no telemetry, over Bolt, Unifying, Bluetooth, or a cable, though the project states plainly that it is under active development and not yet stable, and you have to quit Logitech Options+ first because only one program can own a receiver at a time.

tools.name: Grist
tools.blurb: Grist is a relational spreadsheet: columns are named and typed, records link across tables without a VLOOKUP, and charts, calendar views, and summary tables come off that same data, with forms, Python formulas, and real-time collaboration included on the free plan; the honest limit is that free hosting stops at 5,000 records per document and 10 members, so a tracker that keeps growing means either $10 per user per month or running the free open-source Community Edition on your own machine.

tools.name: LocalSend
tools.blurb: Install it on the phone and the computer, pick the files, tap the other device, and the transfer runs over your own Wi-Fi with end-to-end encryption and an optional PIN, and the project states plainly that it works completely offline, that your data never leaves the local network, and that there are no ads, tracking, or hidden costs; the catch follows from that design, since both devices have to be on the same network at the same time, so it does nothing for a file you need to send across town.

tools.name: NextDNS
tools.kind: Set on the router or per device
tools.blurb: Point a router or one device at NextDNS instead of the resolver your provider hands you and the logs become a live feed of every domain each device in the house tried to reach, with the device name and the timestamp, a block control beside them, and settings for where the logs live and how long they are kept, from an hour out to two years; MakeUseOf's Pankil Shah names the tradeoff without softening it, that seeing all of that traffic means trusting NextDNS with it, and the free plan covers 300,000 queries a month before it goes back to answering like ordinary non-blocking DNS.

tools.name: Flow Launcher
tools.blurb: One hotkey, Alt+Space by default, opens a single box that searches apps, files, browser bookmarks, and Windows settings, runs a calculation, fires a shell or system command, or sends the query to the web, with a plugin store to add more; the caveat is that it is Windows 10 and later only, and its file search leans on Everything or Windows Search being in place underneath it.

tools.name: GIMP
tools.blurb: GIMP is a free, open-source image editor for GNU/Linux, macOS, and Windows, currently at version 3.2.4, covering photo retouching and manipulation, original artwork, graphic design and interface elements, and scripted image work through Python and Scheme; XDA's Patrick Hearn names it on August 18 as the way out of Adobe Creative Cloud and puts the saving at $120 a year, and his honest caveat is that the interface takes real adjustment if you have been working in Photoshop, with minor feature differences remaining.

tools.name: Reckon: Decision Journal
tools.blurb: You log a decision with the confidence you actually hold and the reasoning behind it, check in as new information arrives, then record what happened and how satisfied you were, and the app reads back the gap between the confidence you claimed and the outcomes you got, broken out by domains such as career, finances, health, and personal; it is a $1.99 one-time purchase from developer Roland Leth that keeps everything on the device and syncs only through your own iCloud with no account, and the caveats are that the listing requires iOS 26 or later, is not verified for macOS, and the calibration view does not appear until fifty decisions are logged.

tools.name: Deepmark
tools.blurb: Deepmark indexes what is inside the things you saved rather than their titles, transcribing audio in about 99 languages, describing and reading text off video frames, and summarizing pages, so a plain-language search such as the reel with the one-pan pasta trick finds the item even when those words never appear in the title, across browser bookmarks, X bookmarks, Instagram saves, and YouTube Watch Later and Liked; the caveats are real, because there is a single paid plan at $10 a month or $84 billed yearly with no free tier or trial, and adopting it means handing a third-party service your saved reading and viewing history.

tools.name: BentoPDF
tools.blurb: It is a PDF toolkit of more than 50 tools covering merging, splitting and reordering pages, annotations, forms and watermarks, conversion to and from images and Office files, plus encryption, digital signatures, and OCR, and the project's own claim is that every file is processed in your browser and never uploaded to a server; you can use the public instance the project runs at bentopdf.com or self-host it with Docker or static hosting, and XDA's Abhishek Kumar Mishra points out on August 17 that it can even be installed as a progressive web app, while the repository is honest that Office file conversion needs SharedArrayBuffer and therefore HTTPS, that digital signatures need a CORS proxy, and that some modules load from a CDN with local files as the fallback.

tools.name: Joplin
tools.blurb: Joplin is an open-source notebook that holds images, PDFs, audio, math, and diagrams alongside text, clips web pages through a Chrome and Firefox extension, edits in either markdown or rich text, takes plugins and custom themes, and offers end-to-end encryption so the sync provider cannot read what you wrote; XDA's Victor Awogbemila lists it on August 17 among four small open-source tools that save hours every week, and the honest caveat is that syncing across devices means bringing your own Dropbox or OneDrive, or paying for Joplin Cloud, whose plans start at 2.99 euro a month for 2 GB and rise to 5.99 euro for 30 GB.

tools.name: Search Fixer for YouTube
tools.blurb: The extension strips the padding out of a YouTube search, hiding the For you and People also search for blocks, Shorts, playlists and mixes, and videos you have already watched, and it adds display options such as a grid view and lowercased titles; its Chrome listing reports roughly 20,000 users, a 4.5 rating from 86 reviews, and a version 10.1.2 update on August 11, 2026, and the caveat comes from How-To Geek's Ismar Hrnjicevic on August 17, who calls it barebones next to heavier alternatives, trading breadth of options for a light footprint.

tools.name: Explainpaper
tools.blurb: You upload the PDF, highlight the sentence, chart, or equation that lost you, and it hands back a plain explanation in more than 50 languages, with a chat that takes follow-up questions and links its answers back to the paper, plus automatic outlines and key points for the document as a whole; the caveat is that the free account runs on what the site calls basic AI models and leaves out full-paper summaries and saved highlights, both reserved for the $16 a month Pro tier, and How-To Geek's Jorge A. Aguilar lists it among four AI learning tools for students, pointed at complex papers and research documents.

tools.name: Chronock
tools.cost: Free plan, no card at signup
tools.blurb: It reads your real availability across Google Calendar and Microsoft Outlook, turns it into a booking page other people can pick a time on, and syncs events between separate work, personal, and project calendars so an hour taken in one shows as busy in the others; the free plan is thin on purpose, with one active booking slot, one one-way sync rule carrying busy status only, and one team member, and the site is candid that the integrated calendar view is still beta, that Microsoft Teams support and round-robin booking are planned rather than shipped, and that holiday blocking coverage varies by region.

tools.name: OCRmyPDF
tools.blurb: It slides an invisible text layer underneath the images in a scanned PDF so the file can finally be searched and its words copied, works on your own machine with nothing uploaded, reads more than 100 languages through Tesseract, and can straighten crooked pages with a deskew option and strip image noise with a clean option on the way through; the catch is stated plainly by both the project and MakeUseOf's Tashreef Shareef, that this is a command line tool with a steeper learning curve than a graphical app, that it expects Ghostscript and Tesseract installed alongside it, and that Windows users reach it through WSL, Docker, or pip rather than an installer.

tools.name: Microsoft Autoruns
tools.blurb: Microsoft's own Sysinternals utility lists every place Windows can start something automatically, well past the short list in Settings and Task Manager, taking in startup folder items, Run and RunOnce registry keys, services and drivers, scheduled tasks, and Explorer shell extensions, with a Hide Signed Microsoft Entries option to isolate what other software added and a checkbox that disables an entry rather than deleting it, and How-To Geek's Tony Phillips, who found seven Slack background processes holding 380MB of memory after startup and switched them off, is direct about the risk: not everything you find is worth disabling, so investigate an unfamiliar entry before you touch it.

tools.name: Anki
tools.blurb: A flashcard program built on spaced repetition, which its makers describe as helping you spend more time on challenging material and less on what you already know, with the free computer version available for all major platforms and AnkiDroid free on Android, and the catch stated plainly on its own page: AnkiMobile, the official iOS app, is a purchase that funds development.

tools.name: EarTrumpet
tools.blurb: It trades the single Windows volume slider for one flyout carrying a slider per running application, switches your output device from a right click, and keeps the older sound dialogs a step away, installed from the Microsoft Store or Chocolatey, and How-To Geek's Sydney Butler is straight about the limit: it adds nothing Windows cannot already do, it simply stops burying it.

tools.name: QuickLook
tools.blurb: It brings the macOS Quick Look habit to Windows, so tapping the space bar on a selected file shows a preview of images, videos, PDFs, text, code, archives, and more than a hundred formats in all, without opening the program that owns the file, and the project states both its terms and its edges plainly: free software, free forever, no ads, no tracking, no premium tiers under GPL-3.0, but the Microsoft Store build has limited Open and Save dialog support, so the installer from its GitHub releases page is the fuller one.

tools.name: ShareX
tools.blurb: One free utility that covers screenshots, annotation, screen recording, OCR, and quick editing under keyboard shortcuts you assign yourself, capturing the whole screen, a single window, or a custom region without opening a bulky interface first, and its own site keeps the terms to four claims, free forever, open source, no account required, no advertisements, after more than eighteen years of development, while the limit sits in that same description: it is a screenshot tool for Windows, so a Mac or a phone gets nothing from it.

tools.name: FluidVoice
tools.blurb: Dictation that runs on the machine itself, with a live transcription preview while you speak, a command mode for driving the Mac by voice, and an optional local model the project calls Fluid Intelligence for formatting and capitalization, free under GPLv3 and installed by Homebrew or a release download, and the requirements are the honest catch: macOS 15 Sequoia or later, Apple silicon for most models with Intel Macs falling back to Whisper, microphone and accessibility permissions, about 1 GB of disk for the voice model and roughly 3.5 GB more if you add the enhancement one, and no Windows or iOS build exists yet.

tools.name: SpotAngels
tools.blurb: A parking app that maps free against paid street parking, sends a reminder before street cleaning or another rule turns your space into a ticket, and collects garage deals, which is the kind of thing that pays for itself the first time it works, and its limit is geography rather than price: the free tier is real with a paid SpotAngels Plus sitting on top of it, but the map is built city by city, and the company's own site names ten, New York, San Francisco, Chicago, Los Angeles, Philadelphia, Boston, Washington DC, San Diego, Toronto, and Montreal, before pointing to more.

tools.name: Arena.ai
tools.blurb: One browser page that gathers a range of proprietary and open AI models and runs two of them side by side on the same prompt, so you can see which one actually answers your question before paying for any of them, and the catch is printed on the site itself: your conversations are disclosed to the AI providers and may be shared publicly to support AI research, which is why it warns you not to submit personal or sensitive information, while Oluwaseun Bamisile found the free allowance differs sharply by model, roughly five messages on one newer model against about twenty on another before a limit that resets in about an hour, with image and video generation capped at two a day.

tools.name: Quetta
tools.blurb: A Chromium based browser that blocks ads and trackers by default, installs extensions from the Chrome Web Store and Edge Add-ons on a phone rather than only on a desktop, and saves supported MP4, WebM, and HLS video for offline playback, with reader mode, page translation, and fingerprint protection sitting alongside, and Oluwademilade Afolabi names the two costs plainly: the code is proprietary, so nobody outside the company can audit it the way Firefox can be audited, and the Android build runs on Chromium 148.0.7778.217, a version the company's own release notes date to August 4, which means security patches can reach you later than they reach Chrome.

tools.name: KidScreen
tools.blurb: It gives a child a fixed shelf of YouTube videos a parent has added by hand, with no search box, no recommendations, and no endless scroll, and the makers say plainly that it is free because they are building it so families stay in control, which is also where its limits live: it needs a family account before anyone watches anything, every video on the shelf is one you put there yourself, so the shelf stays interesting only while you keep feeding it, and the site names no supported devices, so treat it as a browser page rather than a television app until it says otherwise. It drew 33 points and 28 comments on Hacker News today.

tools.name: Rowboat
tools.blurb: An AI workspace that keeps its memory on your own disk, indexing email, meetings, and notes into a linked knowledge graph written as plain Markdown files and sitting beside a built-in mail client, notes, browser, and meeting transcription, with downloadable builds for Mac, Windows, and Linux and no Docker to set up, and the honest catch is that it brings no brain of its own: you point it at a local model through Ollama or LM Studio or supply your own paid provider key, and the parts that make it useful, Gmail and Calendar through Google sign-in, voice, and web search, each want their own connection before they work, which MakeUseOf's Mahnoor Faisal also found took setup past the install.

tools.name: Hyperspace
tools.blurb: It finds files whose contents are identical and hands back the space the copies waste without removing any of them, using a standard macOS file system feature to replace them with space-saving clones, and both the catch and the argument are about money: the scan is free and shows you the savings first, but reclaiming them is the paid part, at $9.99 for a month, $19.99 for a year, or $49.99 for a lifetime unlock from Hypercritical LLC, which is precisely what the Hacker News thread of 85 points and 62 comments spent the night disputing, some calling the unpriced scan a dark pattern and others calling it ordinary shareware.

tools.name: Write.md
tools.blurb: A writing app that leaves your work as ordinary Markdown files on your own disk with no account and no telemetry, installed from a .dmg on its releases page, and it spends its effort on how the page feels, with appearance profiles covering typography, color, opacity, glass effects, backgrounds, and window borders, optional Vim keys, and spelling and style help that runs on the machine instead of in a cloud service, though the maker is equally plain about the limits: it runs on Apple silicon Macs only, ships no bundled themes so each profile starts from nothing, corrects basic US English and no other language, and syncs to nothing at all, which is the point until the day you want the same draft on a second device.

tools.name: Craft
tools.blurb: A block-based editor for notes, tasks, and documents that lets you drag whole sections into a new order, nest subpages under a project, and keep daily notes, tasks, and a calendar in one place, and the free plan draws its lines clearly: 1,500 blocks, 1 GB of storage, 25 MB per upload, seven days of version history, and 15 AI credits, while XDA's Parth Shah grants it is not a complete replacement for Word on complex formatting, academic references, or heavily structured corporate documents.

tools.name: Rembg
tools.blurb: Cuts the background out of a photo and writes a transparent PNG, working on a single file, a whole folder, or a folder it watches, with more than fifteen models to choose from and a local server mode if you want one, and the catches are real: it installs through pip and wants Python 3.11 to 3.13, and How-To Geek's Nick Lewis warns that the lighter models struggle with fine detail like hair, that repairing a bad edge means opening GIMP or Krita, and that some downloadable model weights carry non-commercial licenses even though the software itself is free.

tools.name: Buildin.AI
tools.blurb: A Notion-style workspace that treats a mind map as a native page type beside its pages and folders, and XDA's Nolen Jonker reports it also carries a timeline view and lets you choose GPT, Gemini, or DeepSeek as the model behind its writing and its questions about your own notes, with the free plan capped hard at 2 GB of storage, 5 MB per file, 300 mind-map nodes, and ten AI chat requests a month before the $10 add-on that raises it to 3,000.

tools.name: AndroMeld
tools.kind: Mac app for an Android phone
tools.blurb: It runs your Android apps in their own resizable Mac windows and handles phone files in Finder while syncing notifications and the clipboard over USB or Wi-Fi, with the honest catch that it needs macOS 15 or later and the free tier is capped by a weekly allowance that resets on its own.

tools.name: Kaneo
tools.blurb: Kaneo is an open-source project tracker with board and list views, owners, due dates, priorities, and GitHub issue sync, free forever under the MIT license when you self-host it, though the free path means running it yourself with Docker because the hosted Cloud Personal plan is $40 a year after a 14-day trial.

tools.name: Glyphi: Speed Reader
tools.blurb: Flashes an imported book, PDF, article, or web page one word at a time so your eyes stay still, keeps your place across Apple devices through iCloud, and builds its summaries on the device itself, and the App Store listing is plain about the limits: the free tier stops at five saved readings, 550 words a minute, and the Endurance training mode, unlimited imports and speeds up to 1,200 words a minute cost $4.99 a month or $39.99 a year, and the listing warns that AI generated results may occasionally contain errors.

tools.name: Legacy Notepad
tools.blurb: Rebuilds the plain Windows Notepad in C++17 and the Win32 API with word wrap, font choice, zoom, find and replace, printing, an always-on-top window, and UTF-8, UTF-16, and ANSI encodings, and no AI anywhere, which is the whole point of it, and the project names its own trade-offs: it is a young, maintainer-led effort rather than an application tested at Microsoft's scale, its background image modes shift with DPI scaling, and Windows Defender has flagged an x86 build.

tools.name: Zen Browser
tools.blurb: A Firefox-based browser built on Firefox 153.0.3 that aims squarely at productivity, moving tabs into a vertical sidebar where long titles are actually readable and adding split view for two pages side by side, Glance previews for links, pinned tabs, and customizable layouts, and the XDA write-up that put it back in front of readers supplies the honest caveat: no single feature here is revolutionary, and Firefox has offered vertical tabs for a while now.

tools.name: Wispr Flow Notetaker
tools.blurb: Captures a meeting locally through your Mac rather than joining the call as a visible bot, then names the speakers and returns a summary organized around decisions and next steps that you can search later, and its own page states the limits: Mac only with Windows listed as coming soon, English only for now, and free-plan use that becomes unlimited on Flow Pro, which the same site's plans page prices at $15 a user each month, or $12 billed yearly.

tools.name: Wondering, learn anything
tools.kind: iPhone, iPad, M1 Mac or later
tools.blurb: Turns a subject you have been meaning to learn into a course of short lessons, podcasts, and exercises pitched at what you already know, with the App Store listing naming the limits: it is English only, it wants iOS 14 or later or a Mac with an M1 chip, and unlimited daily lessons plus up to 15 new courses a month sit behind Pro at $14.99 a month or $107.99 a year.

tools.name: Screen Awesome
tools.blurb: Records a tab, a screen, or your camera to MP4 from inside Chrome, glides a zoom to every click, and leaves the arrows, blur, redaction, and step numbers unlocked with no watermark and no sign-in, and the honest catch is where the files live: recordings stay in the browser's own storage on the machine that made them, and removing the extension deletes them with it.

tools.name: Wispr Flow Notetaker
tools.kind: Notetaker on Mac only for now
tools.blurb: Listens to a meeting through your Mac's own audio instead of joining the call, then hands back a cleaned transcript, a summary, and action items you can search later, and the plan page is plain about the limits: the notetaker runs on Mac only for now with other platforms listed as coming soon, and unlimited dictation plus more meetings kept for longer costs $15 a user each month, or $12 billed yearly.

tools.name: Pandoc
tools.blurb: Turns one document into another from a single command, and John MacFarlane's twentieth anniversary post counts 51 input formats and 76 output formats, so a Markdown draft can leave as a Word file, an EPUB, or a slide deck; the honest catch is that PDF output still leans on a LaTeX engine you install separately, MiKTeX on Windows, BasicTeX or TinyTeX on macOS, TeX Live on Linux.

tools.name: space ocr
tools.blurb: Reads photographed receipts, statements, and forms into a table where every value shows where on the page it came from, and marks the readings it is unsure of as needs_review instead of guessing quietly, with the limits stated plainly on its pricing page: the free tier is 100 pages a month across three sheets, and exporting a CSV spends one of those pages.

tools.name: Voicebox
tools.blurb: Keeps speech work on your own machine, with push-to-talk dictation into any app, speech generation across 23 languages and seven engines, and voice cloning from samples you supply, and the project states its own limits plainly: there are no prebuilt Linux binaries yet, and automatic pasting after dictation is still not implemented on Windows or Linux.

tools.name: Finamie
tools.blurb: Logs a purchase when you hold a button and say it out loud, pulling the amount, currency, category and details out of your own voice in English or Spanish, with the caveat that the free plan stops at 30 voice transactions a month and one default analytics widget, and everything past that is $39.99 a year.

tools.name: ssh.place
tools.blurb: Type ssh ssh.place and you are standing on a shared canvas of 200 by 60 cells where anyone can place a colored block, which is the charm and also the caveat: the wait is 15 seconds per block and survives a reconnect, text is rejected outright, and the canvas is wider than most terminal windows, so you scroll to see all of it.

tools.name: Isopolis
tools.blurb: Draws San Francisco, and only San Francisco, as an isometric pixel city over an OpenStreetMap and CARTO base with neighborhood data from DataSF, and the honest caveat comes from its maker, who says the style was generated by a model he trained and that it still turns some roads into water and invents structures that are not there.

tools.name: Dark Hours
tools.blurb: Rates a location's sky on the Bortle scale and lays out the night around it, giving sunset, the astronomical night window, sunrise, moon phase and the darkest direction to face, but it models light pollution from population data rather than satellite radiance and states its own bias plainly: within about 15 km of a mid-size city it reads about one Bortle class too dark, so assume the real sky is worse.

tools.name: bitchat
tools.blurb: Carries messages phone to phone over a Bluetooth mesh with no accounts, phone numbers or central servers, and uses the Nostr protocol when there is internet, though the project warns that only App Store builds or source you verified yourself can be trusted, and its whitepaper notes the mesh carries a persistent per-device identifier that a nearby radio can observe.

tools.name: Zen Whisper
tools.blurb: Types dictation into any Mac app from a keyboard shortcut with recognition running on the machine instead of in the cloud, free for 3,000 words a week once the 14-day trial ends, and its makers concede that on-device models handle technical jargon poorly, which they answer with a custom dictionary and snippets rather than a larger model.

tools.name: Meshdiff
tools.blurb: Takes two STL, 3MF or OBJ files and renders a voxel diff in the browser, green for added material and red for removed, with tolerance adjustable from 0.05 to 1mm and volume delta metrics; its author says nothing is uploaded to any server, and one commenter reported that multi-group OBJ files show only the first group.

tools.name: Invidious
tools.blurb: Opens YouTube through a public instance with no ads, no tracking and no JavaScript required, though the project says plainly that it does not use YouTube's official APIs and takes no responsibility for the third-party instances it lists.

tools.name: G'MIC 4.0
tools.blurb: Brings the filter count to 644 with six new ones in this release, among them Pixel Stretch and Heightfield Warp, but it is a plugin rather than an app: you run it inside GIMP, Krita, Photoshop or Affinity Photo, from the command line, or in a browser at G'MIC Online.

tools.name: Elevators, an interactive explainer
tools.blurb: Lets you set building height, car count and passenger flow, then watch LOOK, destination dispatch and other algorithms rearrange the wait-time histogram, which is the whole of it: this is a browser essay with simulators inside, not an app you keep.

tools.name: Yamanote 3D
tools.blurb: Puts you inside an E235 carriage on Tokyo's Yamanote loop, where you walk the car, sit down, listen to the station announcements and step off at a stop, with nothing to win or finish: its maker pitches it as calm background for studying or working.

tools.name: EssayKraft
tools.blurb: A paginated writing app with automatic citations, built-in reference lookup and DOCX export, bought once with no subscription and no account, though the App Store listing asks for macOS 26 or iPadOS 26, which rules out older machines.

tools.name: Gander
tools.blurb: Opens PDFs, Word and Excel files, images, video, audio, Markdown and code entirely offline without asking for storage permission, though you sideload the APK from GitHub because it is not on the Play Store or F-Droid.

tools.name: mectrics
tools.blurb: Folds CPU, memory, battery, network, disk, GPU and fan readings into a single menu bar item that stays quiet until a threshold holds, and its own launch notes concede it goes less deep than paid rivals such as iStat Menus.

tools.name: Focus Room
tools.blurb: Put focusroom.club/ in front of any YouTube URL and the video reopens as a distraction-free course with transcript search and timestamped notes, though launch-day testers hit YouTube quota errors and the notes cannot be exported yet.

tools.name: Kaneo
tools.blurb: Runs kanban boards and issue tracking on a machine you own from a Docker Compose file, and its makers state the trade-off plainly: a deliberately minimal design with fewer features than Jira or Linear.

tools.name: SoundGate Guitar
tools.blurb: It listens through the microphone and draws what you are playing on a live fretboard, with an AI tutor that answers questions and builds practice routines, plus a tuner and metronome; it is an Apple-only app, so Android players are out of luck.

tools.name: Yap, on-device dictation for macOS
tools.blurb: Press a shortcut, talk, press it again, and your words appear in whatever text field you were in, using Apple's built-in speech APIs with no model to download and no network calls; it needs macOS 26 or later on Apple Silicon, and Intel Macs are deliberately not supported.

tools.name: CheapFoodMap
tools.blurb: A map of meals under $10 across a dozen featured cities including New York, Chicago, Houston and Los Angeles, with a price-verified date shown on each spot; the entries are crowdsourced, so coverage thins out fast once you pan away from the big cities.

tools.name: tale.fyi
tools.blurb: One link opens a whole book, keeps your place on the device, and lets you swap between reading and listening; an account is optional and only syncs progress, but the library is public domain material from Project Gutenberg, Standard Ebooks and LibriVox, so nothing modern is on the shelf.

tools.name: TokenTown
tools.blurb: Type a prompt and watch a single token travel through an isometric city where each district is one stage of a language model, from tokenizing to attention to sampling; the model is deliberately tiny and its weights are random and untrained, so the words it produces are noise and only the machinery is real.

workflows.title: Set your 2.4GHz Wi-Fi to channel 1, 6, or 11 by hand and stop it overlapping the neighbors
workflows.dek: Three channels, no overlap Gavin Phillips explains that the 2.4GHz band holds 83.5MHz of usable spectrum cut into 11 channels spaced 5MHz apart while each channel is about 22MHz wide, so only 1, 6, and 11 avoid stepping on each other: run a Wi-Fi analyzer in the evening when the building is busiest, pick the quietest of the three in your router's settings instead of leaving it on automatic, move whatever devices you can to 5GHz or 6GHz, and rescan now and then, because in a dense area you can still end up sharing a channel.
needs: An evening scan, not a morning one

workflows.title: Six Windows 11 habits that give back a few minutes a day, starting with one update command
workflows.dek: Six switches and shortcuts Pankil Shah updates every Winget-installed program at once by running winget upgrade -all in Command Prompt, turns on Settings, System, Advanced, End task so a frozen window can be closed straight from the taskbar, opens unknown software inside Windows Sandbox where everything is deleted on exit, mirrors an Android screen through Phone Link, remaps three and four finger touchpad gestures, and keeps Win+V clipboard history and Win+. emoji within reach; two limits are worth knowing, since Sandbox needs Windows 11 Pro and the Winget command leaves Microsoft Store apps alone.

workflows.title: Read the Google Maps traffic layer before you pull out of the driveway, not just the ETA
workflows.dek: Look before you drive Parth Shah taps the map icon on the Google Maps home screen, chooses Traffic under Map details, and reads the color-coded roads around the trip, spotting the red and dark red stretches before navigation begins rather than trusting a single estimated arrival time, then taps the three dot menu after entering directions to set a departure or arrival time and see how the drive should look later; he is honest that the habit pays best on routes you already know, because seeing the jam only helps if you know the way around it.

workflows.title: The five Android settings worth changing in the first ten minutes with a new phone
workflows.dek: Five switches, once How-To Geek's Sanya Shah hides notification contents on the lock screen under Settings, Notifications, Hide content while locked, narrows app location access to Ask every time or While using the app under Settings, Location, App permissions, turns off adaptive brightness under Display, switches off Ad topics and App-suggested ads under Security and Privacy, More privacy settings, Ads, and stops the Wi-Fi and Bluetooth scanning that continues even with both radios off under Location services; the piece is honest about what each one costs, since manual brightness means adjusting the screen yourself room by room, the ad change makes advertising more generic rather than making it disappear, and turning off scanning trims little battery while it does cost some location accuracy.

workflows.title: Empty the Windows 11 Start menu of everything Microsoft put there for you
workflows.dek: One clean launcher MakeUseOf's Oluwaseun Bamisile opens Settings, then Personalization, then Start, and turns off recently installed apps, most used apps, recommended files, the mobile device panel, and the recommendations for tips, shortcuts, and new apps, controls that recent Windows updates finally expose as switches where earlier versions offered none; the counterpoint comes from the author, who left the suggestions running for a couple of days first and found them genuinely helpful in rare cases, so anyone who reopens recent documents all day may want to keep that single one on.

workflows.title: Put the dates back in the Google Photos grid that the summer redesign took away
workflows.dek: Dates back in the grid Android Authority's Joe Maring restores the date markers that Google's July 2026 redesign removed from the Photos home screen: tap the profile icon, then Photos settings, then Preferences, then Photos view, then switch on Show dates in grid, an option that ships turned off and sits several menus down; the fix is partial by the author's own account, since a floating date pill still rides at the top of the screen as you scroll, and the redesign is described as form over function that made the app more cumbersome to use.

workflows.title: Four Waze settings that stop the app from routing you down an alley to save a minute
workflows.dek: Four settings, calmer routes Android Police's Jade Bryan Jardinico sets Avoid difficult intersections to Always under Settings, Navigation, matches the active vehicle profile to the car actually being driven, adjusts the unpaved road preference in the same Navigation settings, and anchors a route by tapping the ETA bar to add a waypoint so crowdsourced traffic data cannot pull the trip through a narrow alley mid-drive; the article does not oversell the result, granting that some of Waze's rerouting suggestions really are helpful and that the algorithm is far from perfect, with the approach working best for city driving and long road trips.

workflows.title: Five tiny AutoHotkey scripts that take the repeated clicks out of a Windows day
workflows.dek: Five short scripts Tony Phillips uses AutoHotkey v2.0, free and open source for Windows, to bind Ctrl+Alt+W to open a set of sites at once, Ctrl+Alt+D to create and open a folder named for today's date, Ctrl+Shift+G to search whatever text is highlighted, a short code such as eaddr to expand into a full address, and Ctrl+Alt+T to keep a window on top of the others; he warns that the search script replaces whatever is already on the Windows clipboard, so do not fire it while you are holding something you need.

workflows.title: Put related Excel tables into the Data Model and stop maintaining lookup formulas
workflows.dek: One workbook, real relationships Yasir Mahmood describes Excel's Data Model as a compressed relational store held inside the workbook itself: tick Add this data to the Data Model when you build a PivotTable, drag matching keys onto each other in Power Pivot's Diagram View, and a single PivotTable can then reach every related table through the Field List, with DAX measures for the harder calculations; he is candid that these relationships are not database-enforced, that the join fields have to share a data type, and that past a certain size a spreadsheet buckles as a system of record.
needs: A shared key column in each

workflows.title: Put the forgotten USB port on your router to work as shared storage, a print server, or a backup line
workflows.dek: Five jobs, one port Afam Onyimadu walks through turning a router's USB port into network storage every device in the house can reach, a print server for a single USB printer, a cellular failover line using a tethered phone or USB modem, remote file access over FTP with optional DDNS, and a DLNA media server for the TV; he is straight about the limits, since support varies by manufacturer and printer compatibility is especially patchy, permissions and redundancy fall well short of a real NAS, and remote FTP needs secure sharing turned on rather than anonymous access.
needs: A router with a USB port
A USB drive, printer, or modem

workflows.title: Four Android Auto settings that keep your hands off the phone for the whole drive
workflows.dek: Set once, every drive Patrick O'Rourke sets Android Auto to start Always rather than only if it was used on the last drive, turns on automatic music playback so nothing needs tapping on the way out of the driveway, enables Silence Notifications While Driving under Safety and Emergency so Bluetooth and motion detection trigger it, and moves the media controls nearer the driver under Change Layout; the tradeoff he names is real, because bringing media within reach pushes Google Maps and Waze to the far side of the screen, and he calls Gemini's voice responses frustratingly unreliable.

workflows.title: Stop swiping apps closed, and restrict only the few that actually misbehave in the background
workflows.dek: Restrict, do not swipe Brandon Miniman makes the case that clearing the recents list forces a cold start that spikes the processor to nearly 100 percent, where waking an app from hibernation spikes it to about 50 percent, so on a modern phone, which he says should carry at least 8GB of RAM, he leaves apps alone and instead opens Settings, then Apps, then the offender, then Battery (Restricted on Samsung Galaxy phones), and turns off background usage for that one app; he warns plainly that a restricted app may misbehave or drop notifications, and he still swipes away anything frozen or glitching.
needs: A short list of suspect apps

workflows.title: Move your notes into a plain Markdown folder and let Syncthing carry it between your devices
workflows.dek: One folder, no database Anurag Singh left Notion for ordinary .md files in a regular folder, with subfolders only where he wants them, edited in VSCode or an alternative like Cursor, Antigravity, Zed, or Neovim, then installed Syncthing on each device, paired them by device ID, and shared that one folder so a change on one machine lands on the others; he is candid about the limits, since Syncthing synchronizes rather than backs up, a deletion travels to every device, and editing the same file on two devices that are out of contact leaves you with a conflict copy.
needs: A text editor you already like
One folder to hold the .md files
A separate backup of that folder

workflows.title: Clean four things in the raw data before you build the PivotTable that has to read it
workflows.dek: Enrich, classify, split, trim Tony Phillips runs a sales table through four functions before any PivotTable exists: XLOOKUP pulls product names and categories in from a second table, IF turns transaction amounts into High Value and Standard labels, TEXTSPLIT breaks a combined Chicago | IL | Midwest field into city, state, and region columns, and TRIM strips the stray spaces that would otherwise scatter one customer across several rows.
needs: A raw data sheet to tidy
A lookup table of product details

workflows.title: Set up Chrome's own remote desktop for the five-minute job you left on the other computer
workflows.dek: One code, or a PIN Afam Onyimadu sets up Chrome Remote Desktop two ways, a one-time access code for a quick share and a registered host with a PIN for passwordless return visits, and he is straight about the cost: the host has to stay powered on, online, and out of sleep, which drains a laptop battery and raises CPU temperatures, so he keeps it for grabbing a forgotten file rather than a full day of remote work.
needs: Hands-on setup at the host PC
The host left awake and online

workflows.title: Reclaim Android storage with the four tools already on the phone instead of a cleaner app
workflows.dek: Clean, trash, photos, cache Goran Damnjanovic drops the third-party cleaner apps for four things already installed: the Clean tab in Files by Google or Samsung's My Files, the trash folder most people never empty, Free Up Space On This Device in Google Photos, and clearing individual app caches under Settings, Storage, Apps, which together freed about 23GB in his own testing.
needs: Files by Google or Samsung My Files

workflows.title: Four free DNS services, each better at one job than Google's or Cloudflare's
workflows.dek: Pick by the problem Pankil Shah lines up AdGuard DNS for stopping ads and trackers at the lookup itself, Quad9 for malware and phishing, screened against threat intelligence from more than 20 cybersecurity organizations by a Swiss nonprofit that promises to collect no user data, CleanBrowsing for households that want adult content blocked and SafeSearch forced on, and Mullvad's dns.mullvad.net, a strict no-logs resolver offered in adblock, base, extended, family, and all-in-one variants; he is straight about the tradeoffs, since AdGuard cannot touch ads served from the same domain as the page and needs its paid app for ads inside other apps, and CleanBrowsing's filtering is blunt enough to catch legitimate sites while whitelisting stays on the paid plans.
needs: Your router or device DNS settings
One device to test on first

workflows.title: Five Android safety settings that ask for help when you cannot
workflows.dek: Set up the check-in first Roydon Cerejo starts in Google's Personal Safety app, where Safety Check asks you to confirm you are fine after a set time and, if you never answer, tells your emergency contacts your last known location, and can also alert them when the battery falls below 15 percent; from there he turns on Emergency SOS, which triggers on five or more rapid presses of the power button on Android 13 and later and can record a clip to the cloud, Car Crash Detection on a Pixel 4a or newer, Digital Wellbeing's Heads Up nudge for people who scroll while walking, and screen time reminders that appear after 15 to 20 minutes in one app; he does not oversell any of it, calling Heads Up wildly inconsistent across several phones and noting that Safety Check has no home screen widget.

workflows.title: Turn a webcam and two desk lamps into a document scanner that makes real PDFs
workflows.dek: Square the camera first Jorge A. Aguilar mounts a webcam, 4K if you have one and 1080p if you do not, on a copy stand, a heavy desk clamp, or a rigid mini tripod, sets the lens at 90 degrees and parallel to the page, locks manual focus where the camera allows it, and lights the paper with two lamps so one side is not brighter than the other, then lets Camscan, a free MIT-licensed app with Windows and Linux builds, find the page edges in the live video, reorder, rotate, or drop pages, and export the batch as one PDF; he says plainly that a webcam scanner is not going to match a flatbed on every job, and that the more complicated scans, photographs and fine print, are not going to look amazing.
needs: A copy stand, clamp, or tripod

workflows.title: Six router changes that fix slow Wi-Fi before you spend anything on new hardware
workflows.dek: Placement first, then bands Monica J. White moves the router to a central, elevated spot outside a closed cabinet and tests the weak rooms before and after, assigns undemanding devices to 2.4GHz and speed-sensitive ones to 5GHz instead of trusting automatic band steering, narrows the 2.4GHz channel width to 20MHz for stability, splits the two bands into separate network names rather than one Smart Connect SSID, and turns off DFS channels or pins 5GHz to channels 36 to 48 or 149 to 165 for homes near an airport, coastline, or weather radar; the piece warns never to disable 2.4GHz entirely, since some devices need its longer range, and notes that some ISP-supplied routers will not allow a firmware update at all.
needs: One room that drops the signal

workflows.title: Turn off the two background scanners that quietly drain an Android phone overnight
workflows.dek: Two switches under Location Robin John turns off Wi-Fi scanning and Bluetooth scanning under Settings, Location, Location services on a Pixel, where Samsung's One UI keeps them in the same place, and reports overnight drain falling from around five or six percent to closer to three over two weeks; the cost is real, because Find Hub depends on those scanners to track devices and indoor accuracy suffers enough that Google Maps landed on the wrong side of a building and ride-hailing apps took longer to pin down a pickup, so the piece suggests turning off Wi-Fi scanning alone if you pair new accessories often.
needs: Two weeks to judge the result

workflows.title: Seven built-in camera tools that copy text off paper and build multipage PDFs
workflows.dek: Point, then copy the text Jade Bryan Jardinico stays inside tools the phone already has: the Samsung camera's text button lifts words straight off a page to paste elsewhere, the Scan toggle turns detected paper borders into a multipage PDF with Add Scan, Google Drive does the scanning job on a Pixel, and Bixby Vision reads printed text aloud or names a color at a stated 85 to 90 percent accuracy; the write-up is candid that multi-column layouts and irregular typography make the text capture miss lines, so reframe and work in smaller batches, that low light throws the color reading off, and that several of the seven are Samsung One UI features with a Google Drive or Gemini workaround elsewhere.
needs: Google Drive or Samsung One UI

workflows.title: Find the hidden bloat that makes an Excel workbook take forever to open
workflows.dek: Ctrl+End tells the truth Tony Phillips presses Ctrl+End to see where Excel thinks the data ends and deletes the empty rows and columns beyond it, clears obsolete defined names and broken external links out of Formulas, Name Manager, hunts down volatile functions such as NOW, TODAY, RAND, OFFSET, and INDIRECT, checks Data, Queries and Connections for links nobody uses, and renames a copy of the .xlsx to .zip to look inside xl/media for oversized embedded images; he warns you to back up first, to confirm nothing you delete is referenced by a formula, chart, or macro, and that the zip inspection does not work on binary .xlsb files.
needs: A backup copy of the workbook

workflows.title: Three Chrome privacy switches, and a plain account of what they still cannot do for you
workflows.dek: Cookies, location, then HTTPS Oluwaseun Bamisile blocks third-party cookies under Settings, Privacy and security, sets Site settings, Location to the option that stops sites seeing where you are, and turns on Always use secure connections under Security, then says outright what none of it accomplishes: it cannot hide an IP address, cannot match what a VPN gives you on an untrusted network, and cannot stop tracking that follows your accounts, your device habits, or the location inferred from your IP alone.

workflows.title: Nine commands that tell you where a Windows internet problem actually is before you call anyone
workflows.dek: Ping outward, one step at a time Pankil Shah works from the router out: ping 192.168.0.1 or 192.168.1.1 to prove the router answers, ping 8.8.8.8 to skip DNS entirely, ping google.com to test name resolution, then nslookup google.com and nslookup google.com 8.8.8.8 to see whether your own DNS server is the fault, ipconfig /flushdns to clear a bad cache, and tracert google.com to find where the delay begins; netsh winsock reset and netsh int ip reset come last and want a restart afterward, and none of it repairs failed hardware or an ISP outage.

workflows.title: Let Windows empty its own temp files, Recycle Bin, and stale downloads on a schedule you choose
workflows.dek: Storage Sense, switched on Settings, then System, then Storage turns on automatic user content cleanup, which clears the Recycle Bin after 30 days by default and can put the Downloads folder, which otherwise never deletes anything, on a 1, 14, 30, or 60 day timer.

workflows.title: Trade a slice of your top speed for video calls that stop freezing for everyone in the house
workflows.dek: Quality of Service, deliberately XDA's Ty Sherback turned on QoS in a TP-Link Archer router, entered the real upload and download figures from the ISP, set priority percentages, and flagged the devices that matter, accepting a lower ceiling because QoS drops the router into software forwarding that consumer silicon cannot push gigabit traffic through.
needs: A router with a QoS setting
Your ISP's real up and down speeds
A bufferbloat test, before and after

workflows.title: Turn on the taskbar right-click that force-quits a frozen app without opening Task Manager
workflows.dek: One toggle, then every taskbar Windows 11 hides an End Task switch under Settings, System, Advanced (For developers on some builds), and How-To Geek's Tony Phillips is clear about the cost: it kills the process outright rather than asking it to close, it takes every window of that app at once, and unsaved work goes with it.

workflows.title: Four prompts that turn Claude from an explainer into flashcards, diagrams, and simulations you study with
workflows.dek: Build it, do not read it Abhijith N Arjunan asks for an interactive flashcard deck that self-grades and resurfaces every card you miss before the session ends, a step-through diagram that moves one stage at a time rather than arriving as a single static image, and a slider-driven simulation you can drag to watch one variable change the outcome in real time, then leans on Claude's /learn skill to shape the language for learning; he warns that the step-through diagrams cost more tokens and time than the flashcards, and that concern over source fidelity sends him elsewhere for video and audio material.
needs: A subject you are trying to learn
The four prompts from the piece

workflows.title: Collapse a scattered task system into one Google Keep note with dated and themed sections
workflows.dek: One note, many sections Andy Walker dumps practically everything that crosses his mind into a single Keep note, then splits the task half into recurring work, what is due this month, what is due this week, and a line for each weekday kept a week ahead, moves anything unfinished into the section where it now belongs instead of reshuffling the whole list, and keeps a block for undated jobs plus themed dumps for car maintenance, meal planning, research ideas, and finances; he concedes the note has no alarms or integrations, needs daily discipline, and sends anything heavier to Notion, Samsung Food, or Raindrop.io.
needs: Google Keep on phone or web
Ten minutes to lay out sections
A daily habit of updating it

workflows.title: Export a spreadsheet to CSV and have an AI assistant hand back a single-file app that works offline
workflows.dek: CSV first, then prompt Tony Phillips exports the workbook as CSV so the formatting and formulas fall away and only the fields remain, here 5,000 personal finance transactions carrying id, date, amount, description, category, budget group, account name, and account type, then hands the identical request to Gemini, Claude, and Copilot: one HTML file with search, filtering, sorting, pagination, add, edit and delete, summary dashboards, and data that persists locally; Gemini and Claude both returned working apps and Copilot did not, and neither working app handled filters that depend on one another.
needs: An AI assistant, Gemini or Claude
A web browser to open the file

workflows.title: Find out what is actually slowing a Windows PC before you buy anything to fix it
workflows.dek: Measure, then fix Tashreef Shareef starts with AppControl, which keeps seven days of CPU, GPU, memory, disk, and temperature history so yesterday's slowdown can still be traced to its cause, then uses Wintoys to review apps, background services, system tweaks, and storage cleanup from one window, CrystalDiskMark to settle whether the drive is the bottleneck with sequential and random 4K tests, and Microsoft PC Manager for the plain work of clearing temporary files and uninstalling leftovers; all four are free, and the piece flags that Wintoys is closed source and that its developer has mentioned future paid premium features, none of which have appeared yet.

workflows.title: Cut a 300-a-day notification pile down to the alerts you actually want
workflows.dek: Five passes, one system Vishwamoorthy Ramakrishnan turns notifications off outright for rarely opened apps by long-pressing the icon and going through App Info to Notifications, then splits the apps worth keeping into their own categories so an order update arrives and the promotion behind it does not, gives the categories that matter distinct sounds so the phone can be read without looking at it, switches on the snooze button to push an alert up to two hours out, and enables notification history to recover anything swiped away in the last 24 hours; the warning attached is that snoozing and history are off by default and sit behind differently named menus on Pixel and Samsung phones.

workflows.title: Build a one-tap travel mode on a Samsung Galaxy so the phone changes its own rules
workflows.dek: Set once, reuse always T.M. Amrita opens Settings, then Modes and Routines, adds a custom mode, and decides inside it which apps and notifications get through, what the display does, and how do not disturb behaves, optionally attaching if-then routines so the mode switches itself on, then puts it on the home screen or in the notification panel so one tap flips the whole phone into it; the setup happens once and is reused every trip, and Amrita notes newer Galaxy models label the feature differently and that phones without it need a third-party automation app such as IFTTT.
needs: A home screen or panel slot

workflows.title: Five habits that turn a Gemini Notebook study guide from a generic summary into something you can study from
workflows.dek: Sources first Saikat Basu keeps one notebook per topic rather than one pile, unchecks the sources that do not belong before generating anything, states who is asking (student, researcher, casual learner) so the guide aims at the right depth, then refuses the first draft and chains follow-ups such as identify the top three most complex concepts; he previews the raw extracted text to catch OCR damage before it reaches the model and clicks through citations to check them, warning that subtle nuance in legal, medical, or technical material gets lost in paraphrase.

workflows.title: Five prompts that reshape a finished research report into a website, a chart set, a slide deck, or a designed PDF
workflows.dek: One report, five shapes Abhijith N Arjunan hands a finished text report back to Claude with one prompt per format: a single HTML page with fixed navigation and tabbed themes, a set of bar and line charts built with Recharts plus dashboard tiles for standalone numbers, a draggable force-directed concept graph in the Obsidian style, a full-screen slide deck you move through with arrow keys, and a PDF with a cover page, section dividers, and pull-quote callouts; he is upfront that each format still asks for time on what its design demands.
needs: Some HTML comfort to adjust output

workflows.title: Stop the ISP box and your own router from fighting by putting one of them in bridge mode
workflows.dek: One router in charge Oliver Haslam explains that leaving both boxes routing gives you two DHCP servers handing out duplicate addresses, two firewalls, competing Wi-Fi networks, and double NAT, which he says can make it impossible for devices to connect to online services; his preferred fix is bridge mode, sometimes labeled modem mode, which switches off the ISP box's routing, Wi-Fi, and firewall and leaves the modem doing modem work, with a DMZ plus a static IP or access point mode as fallbacks, and he notes that not every ISP router offers bridge mode because some providers disable it to keep support simple.

workflows.title: Plan the trip on a laptop, then hand the finished route to the phone you will navigate with
workflows.dek: Big screen first Andy Betts drags points on a desktop route to build his own detours, drops a pin and uses the travel time tool to see everywhere within a set walking or driving distance, saves restaurants and stops into lists while he researches, and keeps several tabs open to compare alternate routes and times together, then sends the finished route to his phone with a button or a shareable link, and he notes the whole handoff rests on the account syncing between the two devices.
needs: One Google account on both devices

workflows.title: Six settings changes that make an aging Windows PC feel quicker without buying any hardware
workflows.dek: Six free toggles Goran Damnjanovic switches off animation effects under Settings, Accessibility, Visual effects, clears programs out of Settings, Apps, Startup, debloats with a utility such as Chris Titus' WinUtil or simply removes Copilot, which he says can use around 500MB of RAM in the background, disables services an underpowered machine does not need, sets the power mode to best performance, and turns off online Bing results in Windows Search; he is candid that older and weaker PCs gain far more from all of this than new ones, and that best performance runs hotter and shortens battery life.

workflows.title: Write the rules once and let the Downloads folder file itself by type, year, and month
workflows.dek: If this, then filed Tashreef Shareef points File Juggler at his Downloads folder and writes each rule as a plain condition and action, if the extension is .pdf, then move the file, then uses date variables so the destination builds its own year and month subfolders, ending with more than five rules covering PDFs, images, installers, archives, and Markdown files; the program can also match on filename patterns, file size, modification date, and keywords inside a document, and MakeUseOf puts the cost at a $40 perpetual license after a 30 day trial that keeps working with upgrade popups.
needs: File Juggler, $40 after a 30 day trial

workflows.title: Move the router off the floor and away from the fridge before you buy a new one
workflows.dek: Height beats hardware Samarveer Singh had already split the 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands and let his provider's app pick channels, yet a laptop pulling the full 300 Mbps over a cable managed only about 50 Mbps over Wi-Fi, so he took the router off a three foot chest standing beside the refrigerator and put it on a wall shelf up near the ceiling, which left every room a single wall's thickness from the signal and steadied televisions that had been struggling, and he is careful to say placement is one of three factors alongside the hardware itself and its settings.
needs: A higher spot away from metal
A speed test before and after

workflows.title: Turn off three Samsung settings and the keyboard stops feeling a half step behind you
workflows.dek: Three toggles, one keyboard Brandon Miniman opens the keyboard's settings cog and switches off Character preview and Vibration under Swipe, touch and feedback, Touch feedback, then unlocks Developer Options by tapping Build number seven times under Settings, About phone, Software information and drops Window animation scale, Transition animation scale, and Animator duration scale to 0.5x, and he is candid that typing still does not match Gboard on a Pixel or the iOS keyboard.
needs: Developer Options, for the third step

workflows.title: Turn off four Android Auto defaults so the car stops blasting music and reading your texts to the passenger seat
workflows.dek: Four toggles, one drive Jorge A. Aguilar switches off Start music automatically under Settings, Android Auto, General, so plugging in stops greeting him with whatever was playing last at full volume, turns off Show first line of messages and Play AI message summaries under Connected devices, Android Auto, Messaging, because nobody wants a personal or embarrassing text suddenly splashed across the dashboard, moves Day and Night mode for maps from Automatic to Day in the Android Auto app after the system got stuck in night mode so dark the navigation map was basically unreadable, and raises the Speech rate slider under Settings, Accessibility, Text to speech output, since Google's engine ships at a pretty slow speaking rate, and he is careful to add that these defaults are not wrong for everyone.
needs: An Android phone with Android Auto

workflows.title: Sort a backlog of saved articles into act now, reference, archive, and delete in a single pass
workflows.dek: Four buckets, one pass Saikat Basu points Claude Desktop at his Obsidian folder through its filesystem connector, has it read all 500 clips at once instead of one at a time, sorts them into Act now, Reference, Archive, and Delete by weighing each clip against his current project notes, asks what themes run across the whole collection, and finds 50 worth keeping, then spends about fifteen minutes reading the result himself before anything moves, which is where he plants the warnings: the sort was a first pass, not a final answer, outdated or loosely defined project notes will make Claude hallucinate current relevance, code snippets, quick recipes, and single paragraph quotes can look like low value to an AI sorter, and his own review caught a clip wrongly marked a duplicate.
needs: An Obsidian vault of saved clips

workflows.title: Replace six utility downloads with tools Windows 11 already installed for you
workflows.dek: Six shortcuts, no installs Afam Onyimadu stopped downloading utilities once he worked through what ships in the box: Storage Sense under Settings, System, Storage in place of CCleaner, clipboard history on Win plus V in place of Ditto, Win plus Shift plus S for a screenshot and Win plus Shift plus R for a screen recording in place of ShareX, virtual desktops on Windows plus Ctrl plus an arrow key in place of VirtuaWin, Phone Link for notifications, messages, and file transfers in place of Pushbullet, and Quick Assist with its annotation, laser pointer, and chat for helping someone you already trust in place of TeamViewer, and he is candid about the edges: Storage Sense leans on OneDrive to make old files online only and clears only what Windows counts as safe, clipboard entries disappear at reboot unless you pin them, Phone Link features vary by Android model, and Quick Assist suits known contacts rather than a service left running in the background.
needs: Ten minutes to learn the shortcuts
An Android phone, for Phone Link

workflows.title: Format every spreadsheet the same way with five Excel tools you set up once
workflows.dek: Define it once, reuse it Tony Phillips builds named cell styles for input, calculation, and output cells under Home, Cell Styles, New Cell Style, then carries the whole set into the next workbook with Merge Styles, lets Conditional Formatting react to the data through data bars, icon sets, color scales, or a formula rule, sets figures with the Accounting, Percent, and Comma buttons in the Number group, writes custom formats under Ctrl plus 1, Number, Custom so a value can read as millions or show a dash instead of a zero without the number underneath changing, and switches off banded rows in Table Design when the stripes fight the color rules already on the sheet, and he attaches his own warnings: the original cell still has to be formatted by hand before a style can be built from it, and conditional formatting treated as decoration makes a sheet harder to read rather than clearer.
needs: Ctrl plus 1 for the format dialog

workflows.title: Turn a spare computer into a private photo library your phone backs itself up to
workflows.dek: Docker, then six commands Jack Mitchell installs Docker Desktop on a spare Mac, PC, or Linux machine, makes an immich-app folder, pulls the project's docker-compose.yml and example environment file with curl, edits that file to point at the disk where the photos and the database should live, brings the whole stack up with docker compose up in detached mode, then opens the library in a browser at localhost port 2283, registers, and installs the Immich phone app so the camera roll backs itself up to hardware he owns, with timeline views, albums, sharing, face recognition, and map data waiting there, and he does not oversell it: he calls Immich familiar and simple to use but not as automated or as feature rich as Google Photos, and the sharper limit comes from a reader underneath the piece, that sharing an album with someone outside the house means exposing the server beyond the home network, a security problem the average household is not equipped to handle.
needs: A spare Mac, PC, or Linux machine

workflows.title: Turn a course syllabus into a working study plan before the term starts
workflows.dek: One Collection per course Nolen Jonker sets up a Collection for each course before classes begin, adds the syllabus, readings, and lecture videos as separate threads that keep the source on one side and a chat panel on the other, has the syllabus thread pull out every deadline and graded component, writes his own weekly priorities next to that breakdown, and keeps one reference Collection for material that crosses courses, and he names the limits plainly: Gistr's free tier gives a full workspace with 300 AI credits a day before the paid plans he reports starting at $8 a month with a 50 percent student discount, video support covers YouTube rather than files you upload, and answers stay grounded in the sources you added unless you turn on web search.
needs: A free Gistr account in the browser
Your syllabus and readings as files

workflows.title: Keep one USB drive that can boot, repair, and scan any Windows PC in the house
